Geopolitics.summary: As Serbia heads toward an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room to maneuver.

Geopolitics.title: Icelanders vote in tight referendum on restarting EU membership talks
Geopolitics.summary: Iceland will vote Saturday in a tight referendum on whether to reopen membership negotiations with the European Union. Reykjavik applied for EU membership in 2009, following a financial crisis that devastated its economy, but a eurosceptic government suspended the process in 2013.

Geopolitics.title: Sarah Ferguson to return to UK after relocating amid Epstein revelations
Geopolitics.summary: Former Duchess of York moved to Swiss chalet during fallout over her friendship with convicted child sex offender Sarah Ferguson will return to the UK after relocating to a Swiss chalet amid the fallout over the friendship between her and her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, according to reports. The pair were stripped of their royal titles in October over the scandal of their relationship with Epstein. According to the Sun, the former Duchess of York, 66, is renting a six-bedroom gated property in the home counties. Continue reading

South Korea leans toward military conscription for women

Geopolitics.title: Icelanders head to polls for referendum on whether to resume talks to join EU
Geopolitics.summary: Icelanders are heading to the polls on Saturday to vote on whether their country should resume talks to join the European Union, years after discussions stalled.

Geopolitics.title: Mont Blanc ultramarathon trail kicks off amid growing environmental concern
Geopolitics.summary: The annual UTMB, the flagship race of the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc week, kicked off on Friday with 2,500 participants. As the race continues to attract more runners each year, local residents are increasingly concerned about its environmental impact.

Geopolitics.title: Niger junta says it is back in control after soldiers' mutiny rocks capital
Geopolitics.summary: Niger's junta said Saturday it was back in control after mutineers held soldiers hostage at a military base next to the capital's airport. Russian forces reportedly helped members of Niger's presidential guard recapture the air base, killing some of the mutineers, according to diplomatic and security sources.

Science.title: NASA's Roman Space Telescope is ready for launch aboard SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket
Science.summary: A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket is poised to lift off with the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on Aug. 30. This observatory is on a mission to usher in a new wave of astronomical discovery.

Science.title: The discovery of the Great Barrier Reef's whale maternity ward
Science.summary: It started with a simple message: "This is the year to do something small for something huge." Now, 17 years later, the Whitsundays region has some of the best protection in the world for migrating humpback whales.

Science.title: NASA Awards First Prize in Phase 2 of Agency’s LunaRecycle Challenge
Science.summary: NASA named a team from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) as the first prize winner for Phase 2 of the agency’s LunaRecycle Challenge, which focused on developing solutions for reducing waste during missions to the Moon or deep space by recycling common materials, like fabrics, plastics, foam, and metals.  The Composites for Extraterrestrial Recycling By Engineering the Reuse and Upcycling of Zotek (CERBERUZ) team, comprised of undergradu

Science.title: Airborne tuberculosis bacteria may mutate as they dry, revealing a target to curb drug resistance
Science.summary: Tuberculosis bacteria released into the air from infected individuals dry out to form infectious particles that are second only to measles in contagiousness. Weill Cornell Medicine investigators have discovered specific mechanisms that enable the bacteria not only to survive drying but also to generate mutations linked to antibiotic resistance. This suggests that transmission involves more than the passive movement of bacteria between people and may be a period during which the pathogen evolves.

Science.title: The universe is still speeding up, but nobody knows why
Science.summary: A major new analysis challenges recent claims that the universe's expansion is slowing, finding that the evidence for cosmic acceleration remains strong. The findings preserve the leading role of dark energy, while leaving scientists with the enduring mystery of what this strange cosmic force actually is.

Science.title: A never-before-seen picture of eagle migrations
Science.summary: In 1899, scientists began tracking avian migration by placing a small ring with an identifier around birds' ankles. Researchers then had to recapture the birds elsewhere, leaving the journey between those points a mystery. Today, GPS tags allow researchers to see every stage of bird migration. The tags are small, have long-lasting batteries and solar panels, and track dozens of metrics. Migration is no longer described as just a theoretical range but rather as an exact map. Despite this technological advancement, the routes of many species in their respective flyways remain undescribed.

Science.title: Scientists melted a diamond and cracked a secret of ice giants
Science.summary: Some of the strangest weather in the solar system doesn't happen on Earth or even in Jupiter's Great Red Spot—it happens in the interiors of ice giants like Neptune and Uranus. Specifically, scientists have long believed that, at certain pressures and temperatures, it literally rains diamonds inside these planets. For the first time, scientists have mimicked the process they believe creates this phenomenon.

Science.title: Strange 'hobbit' species walked more like us than like 'Lucy,' hip bones reveal
Science.summary: Anthropologists studying the hip bones of Homo floresiensis have discovered that its pelvis was human-like, raising new questions about the origin of the enigmatic species.

Science.title: What time will SpaceX launch NASA's Roman Space Telscope on Aug. 30? (Full mission timeline)
Science.summary: SpaceX will launch the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, NASA's next great observatory, atop a Falcon Heavy rocket on Aug. 30. Here's what time it flies.

Science.title: When is the next lunar eclipse?
Science.summary: When will Earth's shadow cover the moon next following the August 2026 partial lunar eclipse?

Science.title: Your sleep may be hiding an early clue to Alzheimer’s
Science.summary: Frequent micro-awakenings during sleep were linked to higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s in healthy middle-aged adults who had no symptoms. The discovery raises the possibility that subtle changes during sleep could offer an early warning signal years before memory problems appear.

Science.title: How plastic welds retain a molecular 'memory' of their former surfaces to strengthen pipe joints
Science.summary: Welding plastic is a critically important part of everyday engineering—especially for preventing leaks in underground water and gas pipes. For decades, engineers have understood that a properly welded joint in polyethylene pipe can be just as strong as the pipe itself, if not stronger. However, the reason for this strength has remained a mystery.

Science.title: Who was Nancy Grace Roman? NASA's next big space telescope is named after the 'Mother of Hubble'
Science.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to launch on an incredible adventure to help scientists explore the great mysteries of the universe. But who was Nancy Grace Roman?

Science.title: Long-term melatonin use linked to 90% higher heart failure risk
Science.summary: People with chronic insomnia who used melatonin long term had a roughly 90% higher risk of developing heart failure over five years, according to a large preliminary study. The findings do not prove melatonin causes heart problems, but they raise new questions about the safety of taking the popular sleep supplement for extended periods.

Science.title: Nano-sandwich photocathode improves solar conversion of CO₂ into ethanol
Science.summary: Czech researchers at Charles University in Prague, led by Pavla Eliášová, have developed an advanced photocathode that helps convert the greenhouse gas carbon dioxide into pure ethanol using sunlight. The new technology solves a long-standing problem of material degradation in water, achieves record conversion efficiency and opens the way toward sustainable production of green fuels. The paper is published in the journal Advanced Energy Materials.

Science.title: Low temperature graphene growth opens a route to sustainable resource recycling
Science.summary: Graphene is an exceptionally useful material for creating batteries, catalysts and electronic devices. Yet producing graphene typically requires temperatures as high as 900°C (1,652°F), limiting energy efficiency and making structural control difficult. To make graphene production more practical, a recent study has overcome this long-standing temperature barrier.

Science.title: Scientists discover why damaged nerves struggle to heal
Science.summary: Scientists have identified a protein that acts like a brake on the nervous system’s ability to repair damaged connections. Blocking AHR helped injured nerve fibers regrow and improved movement and sensation in mice with nerve or spinal cord injuries. The discovery could eventually point toward new treatments designed to shift neurons from simply surviving an injury to actively rebuilding themselves.

Science.title: Galápagos corals show El Niño events are more extreme now than in past 1,000 years
Science.summary: Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño. These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as global temperatures rise, they are becoming stronger and more destructive.

Science.title: Scientists turn one of the hardest plastics to recycle into high-performance engine lubricant
Science.summary: Researchers have discovered a way to turn notoriously difficult-to-recycle PVC plastic into a key ingredient used in high-performance lubricants such as engine oil. The technique could give mountains of plastic waste a valuable second life while making lubricant production more sustainable.

Science.title: Most people would sacrifice some life satisfaction in exchange for a more equal society
Science.summary: What kind of society would you rather live in: an equal one where everyone is just about getting by? Or an unequal one where most people are doing substantially better, but a small group consistently falls behind? Now imagine having to choose that society before you were even born, but with no idea where you'll end up in it.

Science.title: 'Everything is connected': Readers share their concerns about extreme heat's health impacts
Science.summary: Are you worried about extreme heat? Live Science readers reveal their thoughts about Earth's rising temperatures.

Science.title: The night we nearly saw a 'blood moon' (and why I love near-misses in astronomy)
Science.summary: Astronomy is often about being close to extraordinary things without fully experiencing them. Here's why to love partials, grazings, faint objects and other almost-events.

Science.title: Does water drain in different directions in the Northern and Southern hemispheres?
Science.summary: Earth's rotation can influence a draining vortex. So does that mean water in a drain spirals in opposite directions in different parts of the world?

Science.title: Talking to your children about consent and sexual violence can be hard. Here's how to start the conversation
Science.summary: There have been multiple high-profile alleged incidents of sexual violence against women and girls in news headlines this month. Some involve teenage boys.

Science.title: 'It's kind of the holy grail of what is memory': Neuroscientist Steve Ramirez studies the physical basis of memory in a quest to manipulate it
Science.summary: Steve Ramirez , a neuroscientist and author of "How to Change a Memory," tells editor Hannah Osborne about the science and ethics of memory manipulation, and the incredible power of our brains to recall our past.

Science.title: 'It's going to be beautiful': President Trump signs order to create US Space Academy
Science.summary: President Trump just signed an executive order creating the U.S. Space Academy, which will train students for a career studying, exploring, exploiting or helping to protect the final frontier.

Science.title: Strategic irrigation stress can lift lucerne seed yield and returns
Science.summary: More water does not necessarily produce more alfalfa seed. A five-year trial near Keith, South Australia, found that strategically delaying irrigation until plants showed early signs of leaf drop generally increased seed yield and consistently delivered the highest gross margin.

Science.title: New kind of AI uses a fresh approach to reasoning —‬ researchers say it costs up to 11 times less to run than a leading OpenAI model
Science.summary: Scientists say that a new vector-based approach to cognition is dramatically cheaper than standard methods and signal the start of the "post-transformer" era of AI models.

Science.title: NASA’s Artemis II Crew Receives Congressional Space Medal of Honor
Science.summary: From left to right: NASA astronauts Victor Glover and Christina Koch, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, and NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor from President Donald J. Trump on Aug. 28, 2026, for their service during the Artemis II mission. The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was authorized […]

Science.title: SpaceX test-fires Starship Super Heavy booster ahead of critical Flight 14 (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX fired up all 33 engines of its Super Heavy booster to gear up for the next Starship test flight, which will mark the first time the vehicle goes orbital.

Science.title: Australia’s red soil may be hiding a massive clean energy source
Science.summary: Researchers have discovered that Western Australia’s iron-rich rocks can naturally generate hydrogen and that the process may be boosted to produce much larger amounts. If it can be scaled up, the vast formations beneath the Pilbara could become a major new source of low-emission energy for Australia and potentially the world.

Science.title: Dogs may hold surprising clues to human longevity
Science.summary: Dogs and humans may have more in common when it comes to aging than scientists realized. Researchers with the Dog Aging Project found that patterns of small molecules in dogs’ blood were linked to longer or shorter lifespans in remarkably similar ways to those seen in people. These metabolic “fingerprints” could offer clues about the biological processes that drive aging, including metabolism, inflammation, and cellular stress.

Science.title: 2,600 silver coins found in outskirts of Moscow may have been buried by a medieval plague victim
Science.summary: A hoard of silver coins has been unearthed near Moscow, revealing new information about money minting in the 15th century.

Science.title: Earlier swathing opens a new pathway for subterranean clover seed harvest
Science.summary: Subterranean clover's ability to bury its seed supports pasture persistence but makes commercial seed harvesting difficult. The industry relies on aging Horwood-Bagshaw (HB) suction harvesters, which collect seed from fully dry crops after repeated tillage and raking.

Science.title: Diverse portfolio of protected areas key to Mexican conservation efforts
Science.summary: In 2020, Mexico joined 150 nations committing to protect 30% of its territory by 2030 as part of the global 30x30 initiative. More than halfway through the decade, there is ongoing debate about how to effectively expand protected areas to meet that ambitious goal.

Science.title: How everyday household tasks impact relationships
Science.summary: The physical, cognitive and emotional loads of running a household should be recognized when examining the health of a couple's relationship, new research has found. A University of Queensland study examined the "tri-load" of household labor—physical (traditional chores such as washing, cleaning and cooking); cognitive (planning shopping lists, scheduling appointments); and emotional (anticipating, caring, comforting, consoling).

Science.title: How AI‑powered policing is endangering the public's trust in police
Science.summary: Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has dominated the cultural landscape. Uptake across various sectors, including law enforcement, quickly followed, usually with minimal foresight and little to no guardrails, like effective policies or laws, to govern AI use.

Science.title: Centuries of child labor left lasting spinal damage in Dutch children, study finds
Science.summary: Children in the postmedieval Dutch workforce worked so hard that their spines became worn and deformed, with some children affected before they even had a chance to lose their baby teeth, a new study published in the International Journal of Paleopathology finds.

Science.title: Rethinking bluegreen aphid control as insecticide resistance spreads
Science.summary: When an insecticide application fails to control bluegreen aphid, application conditions may not be the only cause. Research has identified resistant populations across southern Australia, confirming that repeated reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides is no longer sustainable.

Science.title: Takeaway cups may be releasing microplastics into your coffee
Science.summary: Single-use paper cups used for takeout coffee and other beverages release millions of microplastic particles when exposed to hot liquid, University of Queensland researchers have found.

Science.title: Many cities buried urban streams. Here's how to bring them back
Science.summary: As many cities developed, streams that once flowed on the surface were buried underground to make way for growing infrastructure. However, as heavier rainfall, extreme weather and aging infrastructure place growing pressure on cities, these buried streams could become part of the solution.

Science.title: Climate policy could learn from people who already live within the limits of sufficiency
Science.summary: Tina Nyfors, who recently defended her doctoral thesis at the University of Helsinki, studied sufficiency, a way of living and a principle for organizing society to stay within environmental limits while ensuring that people have enough. Nyfors directs attention to people whose carbon footprint is already in line with sufficiency and refers to them as the sufficiency class. Their way of life has a moderate climate impact yet still meets their needs.

Science.title: Dog-friendly dining isn't just a trend, it's good for business, new research shows
Science.summary: Restaurants that go beyond simply allowing dogs on patios by offering dedicated menu items for them can significantly boost customer traffic, spending and word-of-mouth, according to new research from Toronto Metropolitan University.

Science.title: Meeting Nancy Grace Roman: What was the 'mother of Hubble' really like?
Science.summary: Nearly a decade ago, I found myself laughing alongside Nancy Grace Roman: one of the most iconic women in astronomy.
